questions.question: What is the difference between == for primitives vs == for objects in Java?
questions.title: == for Primitives vs Objects in Java
questions.direct_answer: For **primitives**, `==` compares the actual **values** directly. For **objects**, `==` compares **references** (memory addresses) — it checks if both variables point to the same object, not whether the objects have equal content. This distinction is one of the most common sources of bugs in Java.

interviewer_intent.testing: The #1 Java gotcha — every interviewer asks some variant of this
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare String values or Integer objects and not understanding why it gives unexpected results
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Integer cache (== works for -128 to 127 but fails outside this range) as a particularly subtle gotcha

sections.title: == Behavior: Primitives vs Objects
== Comparison Rules
sections.content:
| Type | What == Compares | What .equals() Compares |
|---|---|---|
| Primitives (int, char...) | Values | N/A (no methods) |
| String literals | References (pool — may be same) | Content (always correct) |
| new String() | References (always different) | Content |
| Integer (-128 to 127) | References (cached — same obj) | Content |
| Integer (outside cache) | References (different objects) | Content |
| Custom objects | References | Content (if .equals() overridden) |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: For primitives like int or char, == compares the values directly — `5 == 5` is true. For objects, == checks if the two references point to the same object in memory — not if they have equal content. The classic example is comparing two String objects with ==: if they were created with `new String()`, they're different objects so == returns false even if they contain the same text. For String content, always use `.equals()`. There's also a tricky Integer caching gotcha: Java caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127, so `Integer i1 = 100; Integer i2 = 100; i1 == i2` returns true. But for 200, it's false because 200 is outside the cache range. So always use `.equals()` for objects.

Will Integer i1 = 127; Integer i2 = 127; i1 == i2 be true?
What happens if you call .equals() on a null reference?

questions.question: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator in Java?
questions.title: Comparable vs Comparator in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`Comparable`** defines the **natural ordering** of a class — implemented inside the class with `compareTo()`. **`Comparator`** defines an **external, custom ordering** — a separate class or lambda that compares two objects. Use Comparable for the default sort; use Comparator for alternate sorts or when you can't modify the class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Collections and sorting knowledge — very commonly asked for even fresher-level interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Comparable and Comparator do the same thing — the key is natural vs custom ordering, and where the logic lives
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the lambda syntax for Comparator (Java 8+), mention that `Collections.sort()` uses Comparable, and that you can pass a Comparator to override

sections.title: Comparable vs Comparator
Comparable vs Comparator
sections.content:
| Aspect | Comparable | Comparator |
|---|---|---|
| Package | java.lang | java.util |
| Method | compareTo(T other) | compare(T o1, T o2) |
| Location | Inside the class | External class or lambda |
| Purpose | Natural ordering | Custom/alternate ordering |
| Modify class? | Yes (must implement) | No (external) |
| Multiple orders? | Only one | As many as you want |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Comparable is for natural ordering — the class itself says 'here's how I compare to another instance of myself.' It implements compareTo() inside the class. Comparator is an external comparison strategy — you define it outside the class, often as a lambda, and pass it to sort methods. The practical difference: use Comparable when there's one obvious natural sort order, like sorting employees by ID. Use Comparator when you need multiple different sort orders (by name, by salary, by department), or when you're working with a class you can't modify (like sorting String lists in reverse — you can't touch String, but you can pass a Comparator). In modern Java you often write Comparators as lambdas inline.

followup_questions: What does compareTo return — positive, negative, or zero?
Can a class implement both Comparable and have a Comparator?
How do you sort a list of strings in reverse order?

questions.question: What is the Integer cache in Java and how does it affect == comparisons?
questions.title: Integer Cache in Java — The -128 to 127 Gotcha
questions.direct_answer: Java **caches Integer objects** for values **-128 to 127**. When you autobox an int in this range, Java returns the same cached Integer object rather than creating a new one. This means `==` returns true for two Integer variables with values in this range, but false outside it — a common interview trap.

interviewer_intent.testing: A well-known Java gotcha that distinguishes candidates who have practical Java experience
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting == to be consistently true or consistently false for Integer comparisons, not knowing the -128 to 127 cache range
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain WHY this range was chosen (most common int values, performance optimization for autoboxing), and always conclude with 'use equals() for Integer comparison'

sections.title: Integer Cache Behavior
Key Points
sections.content:
- Java caches Integer objects for **-128 to 127** (JLS spec requirement)
- `Integer.valueOf(n)` uses cache; `new Integer(n)` bypasses it (deprecated in Java 9+)
- Autoboxing uses `Integer.valueOf()` — so it benefits from the cache
- Same caching exists for `Byte`, `Short`, `Character` (0-127), `Long` (-128 to 127)
- `Boolean` caches only `TRUE` and `FALSE`
- **Never use `==` for Integer comparison** — use `equals()`
- The range -128 to 127 covers the most commonly used small integer values

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: This is a classic Java gotcha. Java caches Integer objects for the range -128 to 127 for performance — these are the most commonly used integer values, and autoboxing happens frequently in collections. So `Integer i1 = 100; Integer i2 = 100;` both point to the same cached object, and `i1 == i2` is true. But `Integer i3 = 200; Integer i4 = 200;` creates two separate objects, so `i3 == i4` is false. This inconsistency is exactly why you must always use `.equals()` for Integer comparisons — you can't reliably use `==`. The interview question usually shows you both cases and asks which returns true.

followup_questions: What range of values does the Integer cache cover?
Does this caching apply to Long and Short as well?
Will Integer i = new Integer(100) use the cache?

questions.question: What is the difference between if-else if-else chain and switch statement for multiple conditions?
questions.title: if-else Chain vs switch Statement — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: **`if-else if` chains** are evaluated sequentially and support any boolean expression including ranges and complex conditions. **`switch`** jumps directly to the matching case (more efficient for many discrete values) but only supports equality checks. For 5+ discrete value checks, switch is more readable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Decision-making ability — when to use which construct shows design judgment
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a long if-else chain where a switch would be cleaner, or using switch where range checks are needed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention switch expressions (Java 14+) that can return a value and eliminate boilerplate, making switch even more attractive

sections.title: if-else Chain vs switch
if-else chain vs switch
sections.content:
| Aspect | if-else chain | switch |
|---|---|---|
| Condition type | Any boolean expression | Equality only |
| Range checks | Yes | No |
| Performance | O(n) sequential checks | O(1) jump table (many cases) |
| Readability | Good for 1-3 conditions | Better for 4+ discrete values |
| Fall-through | N/A | Yes (traditional), No (arrow) |
| Types supported | Any | int, char, String, enum |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key decision is: are you checking ranges or discrete values? If-else chains are flexible — you can check any condition, including ranges like 'score >= 80'. Switch is optimized for checking a single value against multiple specific options — it's essentially a jump table, so for many cases it's both more readable and faster than a chain of if-else. The tradeoff: switch only works with discrete equality checks — no ranges. When I have 4 or more specific values to check (like HTTP status codes, day names, or command strings), I prefer switch. For anything involving ranges or complex conditions, I use if-else. In Java 14+, switch expressions make this even cleaner.

questions.question: What is the difference between while and do-while loops — when would you use do-while?
questions.title: while vs do-while Loop — Real Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **`while`** checks the condition before executing — may execute zero times. **`do-while`** checks the condition after — guarantees at least one execution. Use `do-while` when you need the loop body to run once unconditionally, like showing a menu or reading initial input before validating.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of when do-while is the right choice — not just knowing the syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the semicolon after the while condition in do-while: `} while (condition);`
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete real-world scenario where do-while is the natural choice — input validation, menu-driven programs, retry with first attempt

sections.title: while vs do-while with Use Cases
Key Points
sections.content:
- `while`: condition first → 0 or more executions
- `do-while`: body first → 1 or more executions
- Don't forget the **semicolon** after `while (condition)` in do-while
- Use do-while for: menu programs, input validation, retry loops with first attempt
- `do-while` is the least commonly used loop but has specific situations where it's the cleanest solution
- Both check the same condition — the only difference is when

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The difference is when the condition is checked. `while` checks first, so if the condition is false from the start, the loop never runs. `do-while` always runs the body at least once, and then checks whether to continue. The classic use case is a menu-driven program: you always need to show the menu to the user at least once before you can know if they want to exit. Another good use case is input validation: read from the user first, then keep reading if the input was invalid. In practice do-while is used less often than while or for, but when that 'run at least once' requirement exists, it's the cleanest solution.

questions.question: What is the difference between String comparison using == vs equals() vs compareTo() in Java?
questions.title: String == vs equals() vs compareTo() in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`==`** compares references (never use for string content). **`.equals()`** compares string content (case-sensitive, returns boolean). **`.compareTo()`** compares lexicographically (returns negative/zero/positive int, used for sorting). For content equality, always use `.equals()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Complete knowledge of string comparison methods — a cornerstone Java interview topic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing compareTo() return values (negative means 'before', positive means 'after', 0 means equal), or confusing equals() and equalsIgnoreCase()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Objects.equals(a, b) as a null-safe alternative, and equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive comparison

sections.title: Three Ways to Compare Strings
String Comparison Methods
sections.content:
| Method | Returns | Case-sensitive | Null-safe | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| == | boolean | N/A | Yes | Never use for content |
| equals() | boolean | Yes | No (NPE if null) | Content equality |
| equalsIgnoreCase() | boolean | No | No | Case-insensitive equality |
| compareTo() | int (<0/0/>0) | Yes | No | Sorting, ordering |
| Objects.equals() | boolean | Yes | Yes | Null-safe equality |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: For string comparison, there are three methods to know: `==` compares references — it checks if both variables point to the same object, which you almost never want for string content. `equals()` does case-sensitive content comparison and returns a boolean — this is what you use most of the time. `compareTo()` does lexicographic comparison and returns an integer: negative if this string comes before, zero if equal, positive if this comes after. It's used when sorting. If case doesn't matter, `equalsIgnoreCase()` is your friend. And if there's a chance your string could be null, use `Objects.equals(a, b)` to avoid NullPointerException.
